choices.term: Πάντοτε τὴν νέκρωσιν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι περιφέροντες
choices.english: Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus
choices.why: 2 Corinthians 4:10 reads 'in the body', not 'in the mortal flesh' (that is 4:11).

choices.term: καὶ καθ' ἕτερον δὲ τρόπον ... παραδέξῃ νέκρωσιν καὶ ζωήν
choices.english: You may also take the dying and the life of Jesus spoken of here in another way
choices.why: The clause opens Cyril's second reading and must be kept.

choices.term: κατώρθωκε δὲ οὐχ ἑαυτῷ ... τὸ ἐπέκεινα τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ὁρᾶσθαι παθῶν
choices.english: It was not for His own sake that the Word, being God, achieved this, that He should be seen above the passions that are in us
choices.why: The Word needed no victory over the passions, since He knows no sin; He achieved it for our nature.
rejected: that he might see and endure the sufferings beyond those within us

choices.why: τὰ προλαβόντα are the verses before (2 Corinthians 4:8–9); πιστόω, to confirm.
rejected: He especially remembers ... the minds of those who came before

pass_a_gloss: [opens inside the quotation begun in the previous section: 'They seemed in the eyes of men'] to have died (θνῄσκω, pf.), and their departure (ἔξοδος) was reckoned (λογίζομαι, aor. pass.) an affliction (κάκωσις), and the going (πορεία) from us a crushing (σύντριμμα); but they are in peace (εἰρήνη), and their hope (ἐλπίς) [is] full of immortality (ἀθανασία).' What sort, then, is the understanding (νόησις) of the sweats (ἱδρώς)? Paul interprets (διερμηνεύω) again, saying thus: 'Always carrying about (περιφέρω) in the body the deadness (νέκρωσις) of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest (φανερόω, aor. pass.) in our body.' We say the manner of the deadness understood here is twofold (διττός), of which one is intelligible (νοητός) and spiritual (πνευματικός), and the other (γεμήν) is taken (λαμβάνω, pass.) as in perception (αἴσθησις) according to the body. For being God and having appeared (φαίνω, pf.) from God by nature, his Only-begotten (Μονογενής) Word made his own the flesh from the earth, and put on (ἀμπέχω, mid.) this mortal (θνητός) and human body, having the rational (λογικός) soul; and what [is] the occasion (πρόφασις) of this? So that he might put to death (νεκρόω) the sin in the flesh, and blunt (ἀπαμβλύνω) the goad (κέντρον) of the inborn (ἔμφυτος) movements (κίνημα) in it that carry off (ἀποφέρω) to improper (ἔκτοπος) pleasures (ἡδονή). And not for himself did the Word, being God, achieve (κατορθόω, pf.) the being seen beyond (ἐπέκεινα) the passions (πάθος) in us; for he does not know sin; but [he did it] as it were refashioning (μεταστοιχειόω) the whole nature of man in himself into a holy (ἅγιος) and blameless (ἄμωμος) life, when he became man and in the form (εἶδος) like us; for he became 'himself first (πρωτεύω) in all things', so that we too, following closely (κατακολουθέω) his footprints (ἴχνος), may have in ourselves his deadness, that is, the power (δύναμις) of sin in the flesh being idle (ἀπρακτέω); [col. 346] and thus we may be strong (ἰσχύω) to take up (ἀναλαμβάνω) also the blamelessness (τὸ ἀμώμητον) into life. And in another manner too you will receive (παραδέχομαι, aor. subj.) the deadness and life of Jesus spoken of here; for he became obedient (ὑπήκοος) to the God and Father, as has been written, even as far as death itself, and laid down (τίθημι, pf.) his soul (ψυχή) on behalf of the sheep (πρόβατον); yet 'he died once for all (ἐφάπαξ) to sin'; that is, on behalf of the sin of the world, for he has been set [as] propitiation (ἱλασμός) through faith; 'but what he lives, he lives to God.' This deadness then, the [one] reaching (διήκω) through the sufferings (πάθημα) even as far as death itself, the initiators (μυσταγωγός) carry about in their own bodies, 'so that the life of Jesus', as he himself says, 'may be made manifest in our bodies'; for they too will live to God the holy and blameless and blessed (μακάριος) life. And that he makes mention (μιμνῄσκομαι, pf.) specifically (ἰδίως) of this deadness and indeed life, for the present the sense (διάνοια) of the preceding [verses] (προλαμβάνω, aor. ptc.) will also confirm (πιστόω, fut. mid.), having a narration (ἀφήγησις) of trials (πειρασμός) and toils (πόνος), which one wishing to fulfil the glorious (εὐκλεής) course (δρόμος) of the apostleship must endure; and no less he will persuade (ἀναπείθω, fut.) us to think thus, all but (μονονουχί) also interpreting for them what he said; for he adds at once what follows: 'For always we the living are handed over (παραδίδωμι, pass.) to death on account of Jesus, etc.' And through these he shows them too gladly (ἀσμένως) wishing to endure the death of the flesh on account of the piety (εὐσέβεια) toward Christ; for the aim (σκοπός) for them [is] not to look at the present things, but rather to look ahead to (προαθρέω) the things to be and the rewards (ἀμοιβή) of the [col. 347] toils. And they make of no account the sweats from the contests (ἀγών), but rather rejoice (ἐπιγάνυμαι) in the goods from above, for they reckon (διαλογίζομαι) the breadth (πλάτος) of the generosity (φιλοτιμία) of God; for on account of this they are handed over to death on account of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in the mortal flesh. And what [is] the life of Jesus? The incorruption (ἀφθαρσία) and sanctification (ἁγιασμός), and great and above the world (ὑπερκόσμιος) glory; for thus it will be seen (ὁράω, fut. pass.) by us at the [appointed] times, when he comes down (καταβαίνω) to us from above and from heaven [as] judge (κριτής); and he will transform (μετασχηματίζω, fut.) 'the body of our lowliness (ταπείνωσις) conformed (σύμμορφος) to the body of his glory according to the working (ἐνέργεια) of his being able also to subject (ὑποτάσσω) all things to himself.' 'So death works (ἐνεργέω, pass.) in us, but life in you.' For the initiators of [the land] under the sun have imitated (μιμέομαι, pf.) their own master (δεσπότης); they too have laid down their souls, so that we [stray numeral 11 omitted] who once wandered (πλανάω, pass.) may gain (ἀποκερδαίνω) the life from faith in Christ; therefore (τοιγάρτοι) [cut off; the sentence continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: “…to have died, and their departure was counted an affliction, and their going from us a ruin; but they are at peace, and their hope is full of immortality” (Wisdom of Solomon 3:2–4). What, then, is the meaning of their toils? Paul explains it again, saying, “Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our body” (2 Corinthians 4:10).

We say that the dying meant here is to be understood in two ways: one is inward and spiritual, the other is taken as something felt in the body. For the Only-begotten Word of God, being God and having come forth from God by nature, made His own the flesh that is from the earth, and clothed Himself with this mortal human body, having also a rational soul. And what was the reason for this? That He might put sin to death in the flesh, and blunt the sting of the impulses inborn in it that carry us away to improper pleasures.

It was not for His own sake that the Word, being God, achieved this, that He should be seen above the passions that are in us; for He knows no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). Rather, He was, as it were, refashioning the whole of human nature in Himself into a holy and blameless life, when He became man and took the form that is ours. For He became “first in all things” (Colossians 1:18), so that we too, following in His steps (1 Peter 2:21), might have His dying in ourselves, that is, the power of sin made idle in the flesh, and so might be able to take up the blamelessness that leads to life.

You may also take the dying and the life of Jesus spoken of here in another way. For He became obedient to God the Father, as it is written, even to death itself (Philippians 2:8), and He laid down His life for the sheep (John 10:11). Yet “He died to sin once for all” (Romans 6:10), that is, for the sin of the world, for He has been set forth as a propitiation through faith (Romans 3:25); “but the life He lives, He lives to God” (Romans 6:10).

This dying, then, which passes through sufferings and reaches even to death itself, the guides into the mysteries carry about in their own bodies, “so that the life of Jesus,” as he himself says, “may be made manifest in our bodies” (2 Corinthians 4:10). For they too will live to God the holy, blameless, and blessed life.

That he is speaking here specifically of this dying, and of this life, is confirmed for the present by the sense of the preceding verses, which recount the trials and toils that anyone who wishes to complete the glorious course of the apostleship must endure. And he will persuade us no less to think so, all but explaining to his readers what he had said; for he at once adds what follows: “For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake,” and so on (2 Corinthians 4:11).

By these words he shows that they gladly choose to endure the death of the flesh for the sake of their devotion to Christ. For their aim is not to look at present things, but rather to look ahead to what is to come and to the rewards of their toils. They count as nothing the sweat of their struggles and rejoice instead in the good things from above, for they reckon how wide is God’s generosity. This is why they are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, “so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in the mortal flesh” (2 Corinthians 4:11).

And what is the life of Jesus? Incorruption and holiness, and a great glory beyond this world. For so it will be seen by us in its own time, when He comes down to us from above, from heaven, as Judge. And He will “transform the body of our lowliness, to be conformed to the body of His glory, by the working by which He is able even to subject all things to Himself” (Philippians 3:21).

“So death is at work in us, but life in you” (2 Corinthians 4:12). For the guides into the mysteries for the whole world under the sun have imitated their own Master: they too have laid down their lives, so that we who once went astray might gain the life that comes from faith in Christ. That is why…
